newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma bombing trial witness links defendants.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma bombing trial witness links defendants.

text.p: A prosecution witness in the Oklahoma City bombing trial testified on Friday that accused bombers Timothy McVeigh and Terry Nichols met twice in the crucial months before the 1995 blast that killed 168 people.

With the testimony of Timothy Donahue, prosecutors apparently were trying to establish a time period in the autumn of 1994 in which they claimed steps were taken by the two defendants to plan the bombing.

McVeigh is on trial for the April 19, 1995, bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building, and faces the death penalty if convicted. He has pleaded not guilty. Nichols was to be tried separately at a later date.
Donahue, a rancher, who hired Nichols as a ranch hand in central Kansas in 1994, identified McVeigh in court as the man who visited Nichols, saying he recognised his "tall, thin" build.

Donahue said he first saw McVeigh drive up to the ranch in August 1994, looking for Nichols. He saw McVeigh and Nichols together when Nichols was leaving in September 1994, saying he found a better-paying job, working for a friend at gun shows.

Robert Nattier, the head of a fertiliser and agricultural supply business, testified that a customer named "Mike Havens" bought 4,000 pounds (1,814 kgs) of ammonium nitrate fertiliser in 1994. Havens is a name that prosecutors claim Nichols used.
Under cross-examination, Nattier testified he never saw the customer calling himself Havens and said he had never seen McVeigh before his court appearance.

Federal Bureau of Investigation agent Louis Michalko testified that he examined more than 132,000 sales receipts from the fertiliser supply company and determined that such a large sale to an individual was very unusual. He admitted during his cross-examination that he had not examined fertiliser receipt sales from any other suppliers.

The government has presented 38 witnesses since testimony in the trial began late last week. Friday's witnesses focused on minute details that the prosecution will use to tie the government's case together.
But at the end of the day the prosecution shifted the focus back to the human suffering of the bombing, putting on the stand two federal employees who lost colleagues in the bombing.

"I wasn't sure what came first, the shaking or the loud rumbling of the building ... then it became very still," said Brian Espe, a veterinarian with the U.S. Department of Agriculture who escaped from the Murrah building by coming down a tall fireladder.
His climb down the ladder was captured on videotape and the dramatic footage was shown around the world.

Allen Radtke, who works at a rock quarry near Marion, Kansas, said he discovered in October 1994 a theft of "six or seven cases" of caps used to blast rock. But during cross examination he said that he did not recognise McVeigh or Nichols when FBI agents showed him photographs of the two after the Oklahoma City bombing. The blasting caps could have been used to trigger the device that blew up the federal building.
The sheriff who investigated the theft admitted under cross-examination that he never looked into the background of disgruntled employees at the quarry.

A lumber company employee, Ellen Mitchell, testified that a man named "Shawn Rivers" rented a storage unit at the lumber company in Herington, Kansas. Nichols lived in Herington, and prosecutors have claimed "Shawn Rivers" was one of the aliases McVeigh used.

Prosecutors allege that McVeigh carried out the bombing in Oklahoma to avenge a 1993 raid by the Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms Bureau on the Branch Davidian Cult in Waco, Texas, blaming the government for the deaths of the cult.
